questions.enonce_markdown: (a) **Two** main mechanisms of depletion of solar energy as it penetrates through the atmosphere;
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Introduction.** Solar radiation (insolation) arrives at the top of the atmosphere as short-wave radiation. Only part of it reaches the Earth's surface, because the atmosphere depletes (weakens) the beam as it passes through. The two main mechanisms are **reflection and scattering**, and **absorption**. (About 30% of the incoming energy is sent back to space by the atmosphere, clouds and the surface, about 20% is absorbed in the atmosphere and clouds, and only about half reaches and warms the ground: these are rounded textbook values.)

**1. Reflection and scattering.**
- *Reflection by clouds.* Cloud tops are very bright (high albedo) and send a large share of the incoming short-wave radiation straight back to space. Thick cumulonimbus and stratus clouds reflect much more than thin cirrus. Dust, smoke and volcanic aerosols also reflect.
- *Scattering by gas molecules and particles.* Air molecules and very small particles deflect the rays in all directions. Molecules much smaller than the wavelength (Rayleigh scattering) scatter the short blue wavelengths most, which is why the sky is blue; larger particles such as dust, smoke and water droplets (Mie scattering) scatter all wavelengths, giving a white or hazy sky. Part of the scattered radiation goes back to space and part reaches the ground as diffuse radiation, so the direct beam is weakened.
- *Effect of path length.* At high latitudes or near sunrise and sunset the rays cross a thicker layer of atmosphere, so more energy is reflected and scattered and the beam is weaker than at the equator at noon.

**2. Absorption.**
- Gases and particles absorb selected wavelengths and convert them to heat. **Ozone** in the stratosphere absorbs most ultra-violet radiation; **water vapour**, **carbon dioxide** and **clouds** absorb part of the near infra-red; dust, soot and smoke absorb visible light as well.
- Absorbed energy heats the atmosphere directly and is later re-radiated, partly towards the ground.
- Absorption is strongest in humid air, cloudy skies and polluted air (for example the Harmattan dust over northern Cameroon and the haze of bush burning in the dry season reduce the radiation reaching the ground).

**Conclusion.** Through reflection and scattering, and through absorption, the atmosphere lets only about half of the solar energy reach the surface. The amount depleted depends on cloud cover, dust and water vapour content, and on the angle of the sun.

*(A labelled flow diagram showing incoming radiation, reflection by clouds, scattering, absorption and the part reaching the surface earns diagram marks.)*
themes: solar radiation and atmospheric energy budget

questions.enonce_markdown: (b) Any **two** reasons for the urban heat island phenomenon;
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Introduction.** The urban heat island (UHI) is the tendency of the air (and surface) temperature in a built-up area to be higher than in the surrounding countryside, by a few degrees Celsius, most clearly on calm, clear nights (see the figure). Two reasons:

![fig-2](gce-al-geography-2021-p2-officiel-cameroun_exercice_1_fig_2.png)

**1. Thermal properties of urban surfaces and reduced evaporation.**
- Concrete, asphalt, bricks and corrugated iron roofs absorb a lot of solar energy by day (many are dark, with a low albedo) and have a high heat capacity and conductivity, so they store heat and release it slowly at night.
- The countryside has soil and vegetation: much of the energy there is used in **evapotranspiration** (latent heat) and the surface cools quickly after sunset. In the city, impermeable surfaces and storm drains remove rainwater quickly, there is little vegetation, and so little energy is spent on evaporation; more of it heats the air (sensible heat).

**2. Anthropogenic (human) heat and pollution.**
- Vehicles, factories, power stations, air conditioners, cooking and domestic heating all release heat directly into the urban air; in winter heating of buildings adds to it.
- Smoke, dust and gases such as carbon dioxide form a pollution dome above the city that absorbs and re-radiates outgoing long-wave radiation, reducing night-time cooling.

**Other acceptable reasons** (use only if asked for more): the geometry of streets and tall buildings (the "urban canyon") traps reflected radiation and reduces the sky view, so less heat escapes at night; buildings reduce wind speed, so heat is not carried away.

**Conclusion.** Cities such as Douala or Yaoundé, with dense concrete surfaces, traffic and little open vegetation, show the same processes: the centre stays warmer than the rural fringe, especially at night.

questions.enonce_markdown: (c) The influence of **three** basin factors on the shape of storm hydrographs.
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Introduction.** A storm hydrograph plots river discharge against time after a rainstorm. Its main features are the **rising limb**, the **peak discharge**, the **lag time** (time between the peak rainfall and the peak discharge) and the **falling (recession) limb**. A "flashy" hydrograph has a steep rising limb, a short lag time and a high peak; a "subdued" one has a gentle rising limb, a long lag time and a low peak (see the figure). The shape depends on the characteristics of the drainage basin.

![fig-1](gce-al-geography-2021-p2-officiel-cameroun_exercice_1_fig_1.png)

**1. Basin shape.** A **circular** basin brings the water from all parts to the gauging point at about the same time: a short lag time, a steep rising limb and a high, sharp peak. An **elongated** basin delivers water from different distances at different times: a longer lag time, a lower and flatter peak and a longer recession.

**2. Relief and slope.** In a basin with **steep slopes** and a high drainage density, runoff and throughflow reach the channels quickly and infiltration time is short: steep rising limb, short lag time, high peak and a quick fall. In a **gentle** or flat basin, water moves slowly and more of it infiltrates or is stored in depressions: a lower, delayed peak. A high **drainage density** (many streams) shortens the path of water to the channel and has the same flashy effect.

**3. Geology, soil and permeability.** On **impermeable** rocks and clay soils (for example crystalline rock), infiltration is small, so overland flow dominates: a high, quick peak. On **permeable** rocks and sandy soils (such as chalk, limestone or sandstone), water infiltrates and travels slowly as throughflow and groundwater flow: a long lag time, a low peak and a high base flow.

**4. Land use and vegetation (use as the third factor or as an addition).** Forest and dense vegetation intercept rainfall, increase infiltration and transpire water, which lengthens the lag time and lowers the peak. **Urbanisation**, deforestation or bare farmland (roofs, roads, storm drains) increase runoff and produce flashy hydrographs: urbanised basins such as that of the Mfoundi in Yaoundé respond quickly to heavy rain with flash floods.

**Also relevant** (one line each): basin size (large basins have longer lag times and lower peaks per unit area), and antecedent soil moisture (a saturated soil, after earlier rain, gives a high peak).

**Conclusion.** The more circular, steep, impermeable and cleared a basin is, the shorter its lag time and the higher and steeper its flood peak; elongated, gentle, permeable and forested basins give subdued hydrographs. Flood managers use these relationships in flood forecasting and land-use planning.
